fraud, including internal control systems, external audits, the 
oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing and the

reform. To ensure market integrity and investor protection in the 
future, the authors make eight suggestions for the market and 
institutional oversight architecture in Germany and in Europe.

This policy briefing explores possible policy lessons from the downfall of Wirecard, the German fintech 
payment provider, then listed in the country’s top stock market segment DAX. In our view, all five lines 
of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another: the company’s 
internal control system, its supervisory board, its external audit, the oversight bodies for financial 
reporting and auditing and, last but not least, the market supervisor BaFin. The slow unravell ing of 
Wirecard is surprising as there were a number of signals suggesting fraudulent behaviour years before 
its eventual revelation. Our analysis finds a root cause to be a flawed market and institutional oversi ght 
architecture, implicating all five lines of defence. In its current form, it is not sufficiently fit to preserve 
market integrity and investor protection. To improve the system, we suggest changes at the national 
as well as the European level. In fact, we understand the Wirecard scandal in German y  a s  a  po t en t ially  
pivotal event for Europe’s capital market, triggering a regulatory reform of financial market oversight 
that ultimately improves its competitiveness among global capital markets.  
Our policy conclusions aim to ensure the integrity of th e capital market by strengtheni ng 
accountability. Towards this end, we propose to improve the information flow to markets and 
supervision, respecting whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources. The 
accountability of external auditors  has to be strengthened so that they have stronger incentives to 
detect accounting manipulations and fraud, which enhances the information value of audits for capi tal 
markets and ultimately the accuracy and credibility of firms’ financial reporting. To strengthen internal 
control mechanisms, listed firms should be legally required to have an appropriate and effective 
internal control system. We recommend that its head reports to the supervisory board, not to the 
management board. Internal control audits should be considered. BaFin needs considerably stronger 
supervisory and enforcement powers in order to live up to its overarching mandate as to market 
integrity and investor protection. We recommend entrusting the agency with broad enforcement 
powers, including forensic and investigative tools. These changes also entail relegating self-regulatory 
enforcement bodies such as FREP in Germany to a purely ancillary, optional function. Along with 
strengthening its powers, we propose to clearly establish the supervis ory agency’s accountability for 
fulfilling its overarching  mandate. This accountability requires an appropriate level of institutional 
independence as well as sufficient resources to fulfil its tasks. Finally, we submit that Wirecard holds 
lessons that go well beyond the German market and oversight system. Considering the negative 
spillovers of fraud cases in a European market and anticipating that national interests may play a rol e 
in market supervision, which also creates unhelpful externalities, we suggest establishing a European 
Single Capital Market Supervisory body (ESCMS). Given that national supervisors are highly 
knowledgeable of the local situation, we recommend integrating them into a European supervisory 
network. A hub -and-spoke architecture with  clear reporting lines to the hub will also introduce an 
element of institutional independence into national agencies and make regulatory capture harder.

Wirecard was initially founded as a German fintech in Munich in 1999. After an interlude o f insolvency in 
2001, Wirecard was listed in 2005 in the Deutsche Börse’s Prime Standard market segment. It became a 
leading fintech company in Germany, focusing on payment and risk management services in the debit and 
credit card business in Europe, Asia and America. It moved up to the Tec Dax in 2006 and, in 2018, to the 
DAX, the top index segment of the German market. Starting in 2015, there were allegations about 
accounting inconsistencies, esp. in the Financial Times (FT) which wrote about a “House of Wirecards”, partly

known as the Zatarra Report, accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. Following this report, there 
was significant short selling of the Wirecard stock, some of which BaFin referred to the German prosecutor 
for market abuse, leading to indictments and settlements.

entrusted with a public mandate. It has been set up as the “first step” in the German “two-step procedure” of

increases in net short sale positions for a period of two months, in accordance with the European Securities 
and Markets Authority (ESMA). It also filed a criminal complaint against a number of short sellers as well as 
the journalist who had authored the January FT article. The FT continued to report on allegedly inflated sales

Wirecard to conduct a forensic investigation. The report was published with sev eral delays in April 2020,

acknowledging that financial assets of 1.9 billion Euros were missing.2

1. MARKETS, OVERSIGHT AND THE WIRECARD CASE 
Capital markets are a powerful instrument to allocate resources from investors to issuers, i.e. firms and 
states. A well-functioning capital market is a key determinant of economic growth as well as of private 
and public wealth. The term “cap ital market” refers to a complex institutional structure, compri si ng 
various contractual arrangements, regulatory or legal rules, and enforcement mechanisms, physical 
and virtual trading venues, and a variety of financial instruments, like stocks, bonds, d erivatives, and 
currencies, owned by a variety of investors. Together with the banking system, the capital market 
provides the financial infrastructure of the economy. As in banking, trust in the proper functioning of 
the capital market is a prerequisite f or it to play its beneficial role. It is, for instance, critical for broad 
investor participation (Guiso et al. 2008). 
Scandals such as Wirecard can destroy investor trust in capital markets working fairly and with integri ty, 
which in turn creates negative spillover effects. Scandals can make it harder for other, non-fraudulent 
firms to raise capital as investors raise the risk premium or choose to no longer participate in the market 
(e.g. Aggarwal and Wu 2006; Kyle and Viswanathan 2008; Giannetti and Wang 2016; Gurun et al. 2018). 
It is for this reason that fraud deserves attention. In essence, trust in the capital market is a (valuable) 
public good. Among other things, it requires assurance that corporate insiders do not embezzle 
investors’ money (e.g. Shleifer and Wolfenzon 2002). 
For this reason, countries’ legal frameworks and capital market regulation aim to facilitate capital 
formation and market transactions and, at the same time, to protect market integrity and investors. 
This typically encompasses f inancial reporting and disclosure requirements, anti- fraud provisi ons, 
restrictions on insider trading and market manipulation, limits on self -dealing by corporate insiders, 
and corporate governance stipulations. However, rules alone are not sufficient. Investors need to trust 
that compliance with these rules is monitored and, if necessary, enforced. Therefore, well-functioning 
capital markets also require effective public and private enforcement mechanisms. Effective capital 
market regulation and enforcement contribute to the development of the capital market (e.g. La P orta 
et al. 2006) and lower firms’ cost of capital (Hail and Leuz 2006; 2009). These arguments form the 
economic basis for supervisory mandates in many countries. To illustrate: the US Securities and 
Exchange Commission (SEC) describes its mission as one “to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, 
and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation” (SEC 2013). In a similar spirit, BaFin’s webs ite  
states: “The objective of securities supervision is to ensure the transparency and integrity of the 
financial market and the protection of investors.”

investor protection as the guiding principles for the analysis in this policy briefing. The goal is to draw 
a number of wider lessons from the Wirecard case. At the start, it is natural to ask: Why did the scandal 
– fraud and deception at Wirecard – remain undetected for so long? Who or what is to blame? Was it 
due to deficiencies in institutional and legal design, supervisory failures, professional negligence or 
(moral) failures of th e perpetrators?3 Common sense dictates that, in the end, the scandal is due to a 
mix of reasons. In this briefing we will try to identify major reasons for the occurrence and slow 
detection of the scandal, emphasi sing the role of institutional deficiencies. These deficiencies can, in 
principle, be mitigated by reforming market and oversight institutions as well as supervisory agencies.4

never be completely prevented. But this cannot and should not be the overall objective of regulatory 
effort anyway, as it would be excessively costly to businesses, and stifle capital formation and marke t 
transactions. That said, well-functioning capital markets needs equally well- functioning market and 
regulatory oversight. Without it, capital markets cannot deliver their positive contributions to the 
formation and allocation of capital in an economy. The Wirecard scandal has revealed maj or 
weaknesses in this ove rsight in Germany, especially with respect to investor protection and market 
integrity. Moreover, we believe the Wirecard scandal holds broader lessons for European capital market 
oversight.

 What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case? 
 
PE 651.385 7 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
This policy briefing explores possible policy lessons from the downfall of Wirecard, the German fintech 
payment provider, then listed in the country’s top stock market segment DAX. In our view, all five lines 
of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another: the company’s 
internal control system, its supervisory board, its external audit, the oversight bodies for financial 
reporting and auditing and, last but not least, the market supervisor BaFin. The slow unravell ing of 
Wirecard is surprising as there were a number of signals suggesting fraudulent behaviour years before 
its eventual revelation. Our analysis finds a root cause to be a flawed market and institutional oversi ght 
architecture, implicating all five lines of defence. In its current form, it is not sufficiently fit to preserve 
market integrity and investor protection. To improve the system, we suggest changes at the national 
as well as the European level. In fact, we understand the Wirecard scandal in German y  a s  a  po t en t ially  
pivotal event for Europe’s capital market, triggering a regulatory reform of financial market oversight 
that ultimately improves its competitiveness among global capital markets.  
Our policy conclusions aim to ensure the integrity of th e capital market by strengtheni ng 
accountability. Towards this end, we propose to improve the information flow to markets and 
supervision, respecting whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources. The 
accountability of external auditors  has to be strengthened so that they have stronger incentives to 
detect accounting manipulations and fraud, which enhances the information value of audits for capi tal 
markets and ultimately the accuracy and credibility of firms’ financial reporting. To strengthen internal 
control mechanisms, listed firms should be legally required to have an appropriate and effective 
internal control system. We recommend that its head reports to the supervisory board, not to the 
management board. Internal control audits should be considered. BaFin needs considerably stronger 
supervisory and enforcement powers in order to live up to its overarching mandate as to market 
integrity and investor protection. We recommend entrusting the agency with broad enforcement 
powers, including forensic and investigative tools. These changes also entail relegating self-regulatory 
enforcement bodies such as FREP in Germany to a purely ancillary, optional function. Along with 
strengthening its powers, we propose to clearly establish the supervis ory agency’s accountability for 
fulfilling its overarching  mandate. This accountability requires an appropriate level of institutional 
independence as well as sufficient resources to fulfil its tasks. Finally, we submit that Wirecard holds 
lessons that go well beyond the German market and oversight system. Considering the negative 
spillovers of fraud cases in a European market and anticipating that national interests may play a rol e 
in market supervision, which also creates unhelpful externalities, we suggest establishing a European 
Single Capital Market Supervisory body (ESCMS). Given that national supervisors are highly 
knowledgeable of the local situation, we recommend integrating them into a European supervisory 
network. A hub -and-spoke architecture with  clear reporting lines to the hub will also introduce an 
element of institutional independence into national agencies and make regulatory capture harder.

PREFACE 
Wirecard was initially founded as a German fintech in Munich in 1999. After an interlude o f insolvency in 
2001, Wirecard was listed in 2005 in the Deutsche Börse’s Prime Standard market segment. It became a 
leading fintech company in Germany, focusing on payment and risk management services in the debit and 
credit card business in Europe, Asia and America. It moved up to the Tec Dax in 2006 and, in 2018, to the 
DAX, the top index segment of the German market. Starting in 2015, there were allegations about 
accounting inconsistencies, esp. in the Financial Times (FT) which wrote about a “House of Wirecards”, partly  
based on whistleblower information about the Singapore operations of the firm. In 2016, an analyst report,  
known as the Zatarra Report, accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. Following this report, there 
was significant short selling of the Wirecard stock, some of which BaFin referred to the German prosecutor 
for market abuse, leading to indictments and settlements. 
After another detailed report in the FT, in January 2019, BaFin requested an investigation of Wirecard’s 
financial statements by the Financial Reporting Enf orcement Panel (FREP). FREP is a private agency,  
entrusted with a public mandate. It has been set up as the “first step” in the German “two-step procedure” of 
financial reporting enforcement. When short selling peaked again, BaFin intervened and prohibited  
increases in net short sale positions for a period of two months, in accordance with the European Securities 
and Markets Authority (ESMA). It also filed a criminal complaint against a number of short sellers as well as 
the journalist who had authored the January FT article. The FT continued to report on allegedly inflated sales 
and profit numbers at Wirecard, backed up with internal documents. In October 2019, KPMG was hired by 
Wirecard to conduct a forensic investigation. The report was published with sev eral delays in April 2020, 
stating that KPMG was unable to verify the existence of 1 billion Euros in foreign bank accounts. BaFin filed 
a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020 and, a few days later, the company filed for bankruptc y 
acknowledging that financial assets of 1.9 billion Euros were missing.2 
This policy briefing has been commissioned by the European Parliament. The paper was written in the 
months of September and October 2020 by the four authors Jan Krahnen, Katja Langenbuc her, 
Christian Leuz and Loriana Pelizzon. We are grateful for discussions with, and valuable comments from 
a number of colleagues who spoke to us or read a draft of the paper: Ray Ball, Jannis Bischof, Joachi m 
Böcking, Joachim Hennrichs, Tom Huertas, Maximilian Muhn,  Christian Laux, Christophe Moussu, 
Eugene Soltes, and Michael Troege. We also thank Elisabeth Roegele and her team at BaFin for 
discussing several questions relating to short selling, audits and supervisory governance in a telephone 
call on September 30. Last but certainly not least, we are deeply thankful for the intensive support given 
to us by Johannes Kasinger, Head of SAFE Policy Center, and excellent research and editorial assistance 
by Patrick Blank and Patricia Breuer.

 What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case? 
 
PE 651.385 9 
1. MARKETS, OVERSIGHT AND THE WIRECARD CASE 
Capital markets are a powerful instrument to allocate resources from investors to issuers, i.e. firms and 
states. A well-functioning capital market is a key determinant of economic growth as well as of private 
and public wealth. The term “cap ital market” refers to a complex institutional structure, compri si ng 
various contractual arrangements, regulatory or legal rules, and enforcement mechanisms, physical 
and virtual trading venues, and a variety of financial instruments, like stocks, bonds, d erivatives, and 
currencies, owned by a variety of investors. Together with the banking system, the capital market 
provides the financial infrastructure of the economy. As in banking, trust in the proper functioning of 
the capital market is a prerequisite f or it to play its beneficial role. It is, for instance, critical for broad 
investor participation (Guiso et al. 2008). 
Scandals such as Wirecard can destroy investor trust in capital markets working fairly and with integri ty, 
which in turn creates negative spillover effects. Scandals can make it harder for other, non-fraudulent 
firms to raise capital as investors raise the risk premium or choose to no longer participate in the market 
(e.g. Aggarwal and Wu 2006; Kyle and Viswanathan 2008; Giannetti and Wang 2016; Gurun et al. 2018). 
It is for this reason that fraud deserves attention. In essence, trust in the capital market is a (valuable) 
public good. Among other things, it requires assurance that corporate insiders do not embezzle 
investors’ money (e.g. Shleifer and Wolfenzon 2002). 
For this reason, countries’ legal frameworks and capital market regulation aim to facilitate capital 
formation and market transactions and, at the same time, to protect market integrity and investors. 
This typically encompasses f inancial reporting and disclosure requirements, anti- fraud provisi ons, 
restrictions on insider trading and market manipulation, limits on self -dealing by corporate insiders, 
and corporate governance stipulations. However, rules alone are not sufficient. Investors need to trust 
that compliance with these rules is monitored and, if necessary, enforced. Therefore, well-functioning 
capital markets also require effective public and private enforcement mechanisms. Effective capital 
market regulation and enforcement contribute to the development of the capital market (e.g. La P orta 
et al. 2006) and lower firms’ cost of capital (Hail and Leuz 2006; 2009). These arguments form the 
economic basis for supervisory mandates in many countries. To illustrate: the US Securities and 
Exchange Commission (SEC) describes its mission as one “to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, 
and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation” (SEC 2013). In a similar spirit, BaFin’s webs ite  
states: “The objective of securities supervision is to ensure the transparency and integrity of the 
financial market and the protection of investors.” 
Consistent with these objectives and the above economic arguments, we use market integrity and 
investor protection as the guiding principles for the analysis in this policy briefing. The goal is to draw 
a number of wider lessons from the Wirecard case. At the start, it is natural to ask: Why did the scandal 
– fraud and deception at Wirecard – remain undetected for so long? Who or what is to blame? Was it 
due to deficiencies in institutional and legal design, supervisory failures, professional negligence or 
(moral) failures of th e perpetrators?3 Common sense dictates that, in the end, the scandal is due to a 
mix of reasons. In this briefing we will try to identify major reasons for the occurrence and slow 
detection of the scandal, emphasi sing the role of institutional deficiencies. These deficiencies can, in 
principle, be mitigated by reforming market and oversight institutions as well as supervisory agencies.4

We realise that, even with much more stringent market and institutional oversight, fraud will probabl y 
never be completely prevented. But this cannot and should not be the overall objective of regulatory 
effort anyway, as it would be excessively costly to businesses, and stifle capital formation and marke t 
transactions. That said, well-functioning capital markets needs equally well- functioning market and 
regulatory oversight. Without it, capital markets cannot deliver their positive contributions to the 
formation and allocation of capital in an economy. The Wirecard scandal has revealed maj or 
weaknesses in this ove rsight in Germany, especially with respect to investor protection and market 
integrity. Moreover, we believe the Wirecard scandal holds broader lessons for European capital market 
oversight.  
In this policy briefing, we discuss four shortcomings of market a nd institutional oversight that the 
Wirecard case has brought to light: Shortcomings with respect to whistleblowers a nd in fo rm at io n flows  
into prices (section 2.1); Weaknesses of external audits, internal controls but also market forces when it 
comes to Wirecard’s accounting information (section 2.2); Limitations in the supervisor’s investigation 
and enforcement powers, limiting its ability to take the appropriate action when needed (sections 2.3 
and 2.4); The potential for negative externalities and the ri sk of supervisory capture in a fragmented 
European capital market (section 2.4). All four limitations give rise to far-reaching reform proposal s of 
the oversight system in Germany and Europe. Those proposals are summarised in section 3.

arguments.text: SRC-002 (European Parliament ECON-commission study, November 2020; manuscript completed May 2020) states: Wirecard founded 1999, listed 2005, moved to DAX in 2018. Allegations of accounting inconsistencies began in 2015, including Financial Times reporting based partly on Singapore whistleblower information. The 2016 Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. After a January 2019 FT report, BaFin requested a FREP investigation; BaFin prohibited increases in net short positions for two months and filed criminal complaints against short sellers and the FT journalist. FT continued reporting allegedly inflated sales and profit numbers backed by internal documents. Wirecard hired KPMG in October 2019 for a forensic investigation; the report was delayed until April 2020 and stated KPMG could not verify existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020; days later Wirecard filed for bankruptcy acknowledging €1.9 billion in missing financial assets. The authors assess that all five lines of defence—internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, reporting/audit oversight bodies, and BaFin—failed in one way or another, while noting hindsight-bias concerns and framing this as an assessment, not a court finding. SRC-001 is Wirecard's 28 April 2020 announcement: it said KPMG found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of 2016–18 accounts; it also said not all data needed to prove TPA revenues could be obtained because data were controlled by third parties, documented organizational weaknesses existed, and E&Y audit timing remained unresolved.

# Wirecard / Jan Marsalek Public-Fraud Trail

## Scope and evidentiary limits

This report uses only information returned by the benchmark tools. The returned evidence supports a substantial Wirecard chronology involving public allegations, regulatory responses, audit limitations, missing assets, and bankruptcy. However, the benchmark results did **not** return reliable evidence about Jan Marsalek’s departure, disappearance, location, or alleged links to any state or intelligence service. Those matters are therefore not asserted as facts here.

The principal sources are:

- **SRC-002** — European Parliament ECON-commission study, *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?*
- **SRC-001** — Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 announcement concerning the KPMG special investigation.

## Executive assessment

The public trail reconstructed from the returned evidence is:

1. Accounting concerns and allegations were publicly circulating by 2015, including Financial Times reporting partly based on whistleblower information concerning Singapore operations. **[SRC-002]**
2. A 2016 analyst report, the Zatarra Report, accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. **[SRC-002]**
3. After a January 2019 Financial Times report, BaFin requested a FREP investigation into Wirecard’s financial statements. BaFin also restricted increases in net short positions and filed criminal complaints against short sellers and the journalist involved. **[SRC-002]**
4. The Financial Times continued reporting alleged inflation of Wirecard’s sales and profits, reportedly supported by internal documents. **[SRC-002]**
5. Wirecard commissioned KPMG in October 2019 to conduct a forensic investigation. KPMG’s report was delayed until April 2020. **[SRC-002]**
6. Wirecard’s own 28 April 2020 announcement presented the KPMG results as finding no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. At the same time, the announcement acknowledged that not all data necessary to prove third-party-acquiring revenues could be obtained because the data were controlled by third parties, and it reported documentation and organizational weaknesses. **[SRC-001]**
7. The European Parliament study states that KPMG could not verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. It further states that BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020 and that Wirecard filed for bankruptcy days later, acknowledging €1.9 billion in missing financial assets. **[SRC-002]**
8. The study assesses that all five lines of defence—Wirecard’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and audit-oversight bodies, and BaFin—failed in one way or another. This is an analytical assessment by the study’s authors, not a judicial finding of criminal liability by each body. **[SRC-002]**

## Findings

### 1. What was the earliest publicly documented warning signal?

Accounting inconsistencies were publicly alleged from 2015 onward. The Financial Times reported on a “House of Wirecards,” with some reporting based on whistleblower information concerning Singapore operations. In 2016, the Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. **[SRC-002]**

These were allegations and reported warnings at the time, not established findings in the returned evidence.

### 2. How did Wirecard and regulators respond to the 2019 allegations?

After a detailed January 2019 Financial Times report, BaFin requested that FREP investigate Wirecard’s financial statements. When short selling increased, BaFin prohibited increases in net short-sale positions for two months and filed criminal complaints against certain short sellers and the journalist who authored the January article. **[SRC-002]**

The source does not establish that the short sellers or journalist committed wrongdoing; it records BaFin’s actions.

### 3. What did the public reporting allege?

The Financial Times continued reporting alleged inflation of Wirecard’s sales and profit numbers, reportedly supported by internal documents. The returned source does not independently adjudicate those allegations, but it identifies them as an important part of the warning trail preceding the forensic review. **[SRC-002]**

### 4. What did KPMG’s review establish or fail to establish?

Wirecard hired KPMG in October 2019 for a forensic investigation. The report was delayed until April 2020. According to the European Parliament study, KPMG was unable to verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. **[SRC-002]**

Wirecard’s own announcement gave a more favorable characterization: it stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. **[SRC-001]**

The same announcement acknowledged important limitations:

- not all data needed to prove third-party-acquiring revenues could be obtained;
- the required data were primarily controlled by third parties;
- documentation and organizational weaknesses had been identified;
- the audit by E&Y had not yet been completed, with its timing unresolved. **[SRC-001]**

Accordingly, the evidence supports describing KPMG’s work as **uncertain and incomplete in important respects**, rather than as a definitive exoneration or definitive proof of fraud.

### 5. What happened to the missing cash or assets?

The European Parliament study states that, after BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020, Wirecard filed for bankruptcy days later and acknowledged that €1.9 billion in financial assets were missing. **[SRC-002]**

The returned evidence does not establish the ultimate destination of those assets, the precise mechanism by which they became missing, or the criminal responsibility of particular individuals.

### 6. What supervisory failures are supported by the evidence?

The European Parliament study concludes that all five lines of defence failed in one way or another:

- Wirecard’s internal control system;
- Wirecard’s supervisory board;
- the external audit function;
- oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing;
- BaFin as market supervisor. **[SRC-002]**

The study identifies broader weaknesses involving information flows, whistleblowers, external audits, internal controls, market forces, enforcement powers, and fragmented supervision. It also cautions against hindsight bias and presents its conclusions as policy analysis. **[SRC-002]**

Thus, the strongest supported conclusion is **systemic or institutional failure across multiple control layers**, not a source-supported finding that every named institution or person committed a criminal offense.

### 7. What is established about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance?

Nothing sufficient was returned by the benchmark tools to establish a fact-based account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The search results did not provide a source documenting his last confirmed whereabouts, date of disappearance, travel, current location, or alleged affiliations.

Any narrative concerning Marsalek’s flight, possible concealment, or links to foreign intelligence services is therefore **outside the supported evidence in this investigation** and is omitted.

## Reconstructed chronology

| Period | Event | Evidentiary status |
|---|---|---|
| 2015 | Public allegations of accounting inconsistencies; Financial Times reporting partly based on Singapore whistleblower information | Reported allegation / warning signal **[SRC-002]** |
| 2016 | Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud | Allegation contained in an analyst report **[SRC-002]** |
| January 2019 | Financial Times published another detailed report; BaFin requested a FREP investigation | Supported event **[SRC-002]** |
| 2019 | BaFin restricted increases in net short positions and filed complaints against certain short sellers and the FT journalist | Supported regulatory actions; underlying wrongdoing not established here **[SRC-002]** |
| October 2019 | Wirecard hired KPMG for a forensic investigation | Supported event **[SRC-002]** |
| April 2020 | KPMG report released after delays; Wirecard issued a favorable public summary while acknowledging data and organizational limitations | Supported, with conflicting characterizations **[SRC-001] [SRC-002]** |
| June 2020 | BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard; Wirecard filed for bankruptcy days later and acknowledged €1.9 billion in missing financial assets | Supported event **[SRC-002]** |
| Undetermined | Jan Marsalek disappearance | Not established by returned benchmark evidence |

## Claims

1. **Wirecard was the subject of public accounting allegations years before its collapse.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

2. **The warning trail included Financial Times reporting, whistleblower information concerning Singapore operations, and the 2016 Zatarra Report.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

3. **BaFin responded to the January 2019 reporting by requesting a FREP investigation and later restricting increases in net short positions.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

4. **Wirecard commissioned KPMG to conduct a forensic investigation in October 2019.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

5. **KPMG’s review did not provide a clean evidentiary resolution: Wirecard publicly emphasized the absence of incriminating evidence, while the European Parliament study reported that KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-001], [SRC-002]**

6. **Wirecard’s own announcement acknowledged that certain data required to verify third-party-acquiring revenues were unavailable because they were controlled by third parties.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-001]**

7. **Wirecard later acknowledged €1.9 billion in missing financial assets when it filed for bankruptcy in June 2020.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

8. **The European Parliament study assesses that all five major lines of defence failed in some way.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-002]**

9. **The returned evidence does not support a factual reconstruction of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.**  
   Source references: **[SRC-001], [SRC-002]**  
   This is an evidence-limit conclusion: neither source supplies the necessary disappearance facts.

## Reasoning steps

1. **R1**  
   - **Conclusion:** Wirecard faced a sustained warning trail before its bankruptcy.  
   - **Premise entities:** Wirecard; Financial Times; 2016 Zatarra Report; FREP; BaFin.  
   - **Premise relations:** `LINKED_TO`, `PUBLISHED_BY`, `INVESTIGATED_BREACH_OF`, `OCCURRED_ON`.  
   - **Source references:** **[SRC-002]**

2. **R2**  
   - **Conclusion:** Regulatory action followed public reporting but did not prevent the later collapse.  
   - **Premise entities:** BaFin; FREP; Wirecard; January 2019 Financial Times report; Wirecard bankruptcy.  
   - **Premise relations:** `INVESTIGATED_BREACH_OF`, `OCCURRED_ON`, `DISCLOSED_MISSING_CASH`.  
   - **Source references:** **[SRC-002]**

3. **R3**  
   - **Conclusion:** The April 2020 audit narrative contained material uncertainty rather than a definitive resolution.  
   - **Premise entities:** KPMG; Wirecard; KPMG forensic investigation report; SRC-001; E&Y.  
   - **Premise relations:** `PERFORMED_SPECIAL_AUDIT`, `LINKED_TO`, `PUBLISHED_BY`, `AUDITED`, `CAPTURED_ON`.  
   - **Source references:** **[SRC-001], [SRC-002]**

4. **R4**  
   - **Conclusion:** The missing-assets disclosure sharply escalated the matter from allegations and verification problems to a confirmed corporate liquidity or asset shortfall acknowledged by Wirecard.  
   - **Premise entities:** Wirecard; Wirecard bankruptcy; 2020-06.

## Scope and evidentiary limits

This report uses only information returned by the benchmark tools. The returned evidence supports a substantial Wirecard chronology involving public allegations, regulatory responses, audit limitations, missing assets, and bankruptcy. However, the benchmark results did **not** return reliable evidence about Jan Marsalek’s departure, disappearance, location, or alleged links to any state or intelligence service. Those matters are therefore not asserted as facts here.

The principal sources are:

- **SRC-002** — European Parliament ECON-commission study, *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?*
- **SRC-001** — Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 announcement concerning the KPMG special investigation.

## Executive assessment

The public trail reconstructed from the returned evidence is:

1. Accounting concerns and allegations were publicly circulating by 2015, including Financial Times reporting partly based on whistleblower information concerning Singapore operations. **[SRC-002]**
2. A 2016 analyst report, the Zatarra Report, accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. **[SRC-002]**
3. After a January 2019 Financial Times report, BaFin requested a FREP investigation into Wirecard’s financial statements. BaFin also restricted increases in net short positions and filed criminal complaints against short sellers and the journalist involved. **[SRC-002]**
4. The Financial Times continued reporting alleged inflation of Wirecard’s sales and profits, reportedly supported by internal documents. **[SRC-002]**
5. Wirecard commissioned KPMG in October 2019 to conduct a forensic investigation. KPMG’s report was delayed until April 2020. **[SRC-002]**
6. Wirecard’s own 28 April 2020 announcement presented the KPMG results as finding no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. At the same time, the announcement acknowledged that not all data necessary to prove third-party-acquiring revenues could be obtained because the data were controlled by third parties, and it reported documentation and organizational weaknesses. **[SRC-001]**
7. The European Parliament study states that KPMG could not verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. It further states that BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020 and that Wirecard filed for bankruptcy days later, acknowledging €1.9 billion in missing financial assets. **[SRC-002]**
8. The study assesses that all five lines of defence—Wirecard’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and audit-oversight bodies, and BaFin—failed in one way or another. This is an analytical assessment by the study’s authors, not a judicial finding of criminal liability by each body. **[SRC-002]**

## Findings

### 1. What was the earliest publicly documented warning signal?

Accounting inconsistencies were publicly alleged from 2015 onward. The Financial Times reported on a “House of Wirecards,” with some reporting based on whistleblower information concerning Singapore operations. In 2016, the Zatarra Report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. **[SRC-002]**

These were allegations and reported warnings at the time, not established findings in the returned evidence.

### 2. How did Wirecard and regulators respond to the 2019 allegations?

After a detailed January 2019 Financial Times report, BaFin requested that FREP investigate Wirecard’s financial statements. When short selling increased, BaFin prohibited increases in net short-sale positions for two months and filed criminal complaints against certain short sellers and the journalist who authored the January article. **[SRC-002]**

The source does not establish that the short sellers or journalist committed wrongdoing; it records BaFin’s actions.

### 3. What did the public reporting allege?

The Financial Times continued reporting alleged inflation of Wirecard’s sales and profit numbers, reportedly supported by internal documents. The returned source does not independently adjudicate those allegations, but it identifies them as an important part of the warning trail preceding the forensic review. **[SRC-002]**

### 4. What did KPMG’s review establish or fail to establish?

Wirecard hired KPMG in October 2019 for a forensic investigation. The report was delayed until April 2020. According to the European Parliament study, KPMG was unable to verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. **[SRC-002]**

Wirecard’s own announcement gave a more favorable characterization: it stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. **[SRC-001]**

The same announcement acknowledged important limitations:

- not all data needed to prove third-party-acquiring revenues could be obtained;
- the required data were primarily controlled by third parties;
- documentation and organizational weaknesses had been identified;
- the audit by E&Y had not yet been completed, with its timing unresolved. **[SRC-001]**

Accordingly, the evidence supports describing KPMG’s work as **uncertain and incomplete in important respects**, rather than as a definitive exoneration or definitive proof of fraud.

### 5. What happened to the missing cash or assets?

The European Parliament study states that, after BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020, Wirecard filed for bankruptcy days later and acknowledged that €1.9 billion in financial assets were missing. **[SRC-002]**

The returned evidence does not establish the ultimate destination of those assets, the precise mechanism by which they became missing, or the criminal responsibility of particular individuals.

The European Parliament study concludes that all five lines of defence failed in one way or another:

- Wirecard’s internal control system;
- Wirecard’s supervisory board;
- the external audit function;
- oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing;
- BaFin as market supervisor. **[SRC-002]**

The study identifies broader weaknesses involving information flows, whistleblowers, external audits, internal controls, market forces, enforcement powers, and fragmented supervision. It also cautions against hindsight bias and presents its conclusions as policy analysis. **[SRC-002]**

Thus, the strongest supported conclusion is **systemic or institutional failure across multiple control layers**, not a source-supported finding that every named institution or person committed a criminal offense.

Nothing sufficient was returned by the benchmark tools to establish a fact-based account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The search results did not provide a source documenting his last confirmed whereabouts, date of disappearance, travel, current location, or alleged affiliations.

Wirecard stated on 28 April 2020 that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. **[SRC-001]**

The European Parliament study states that KPMG could not verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. **[SRC-002]**

Wirecard stated that available documents and audit measures were sufficient to prove revenues in the third-party-acquiring business, while also acknowledging that KPMG could not obtain all data required under its enhanced forensic requirements because third parties controlled the data. **[SRC-001]**

This creates a qualification or tension in the company’s public assurance: accounting support was described as sufficient under ordinary audit procedures, but forensic verification was limited by unavailable underlying data.
